claims.text: The AlCrFeNiSi feedstock has spherical morphology and a controlled particle-size distribution suitable for laser powder bed fusion.
Substrate and chamber preheating combined with moderate laser parameters will reduce thermal gradients during deposition.
Reducing thermal gradients will minimize residual stresses in AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
The proposed processing conditions will promote a homogeneous, stress-relieved microstructure.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi builds will have greater ductility than builds made under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi builds will have greater yield strength than builds made under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
A substrate and chamber temperature range of 300–500 °C is applicable to miniature AlCrFeNiSi components.
Moderate laser power and scanning speed provide controlled thermal input and avoid excessive thermal loads associated with rapid cooling.
Preheating reduces the temperature differential between the melt pool and substrate.
A reduced melt-pool-to-substrate temperature differential minimizes coarse phase segregation.
Preheating slows the cooling rate during solidification.
Slower, controlled solidification reduces residual thermal stresses.
Controlled solidification suppresses inhomogeneous or deleterious phases.
A high-purity inert atmosphere prevents oxidation at the proposed elevated build temperatures.
A high-purity inert atmosphere prevents elemental segregation induced by elevated build temperatures.
The proposed intervention will produce a more robust and simplified process window.
Conventional laser powder bed fusion without preheating produces high thermal gradients, rapid cooling, significant residual stresses, and degraded mechanical performance.
Temperatures above the proposed window may cause oxidation or segregation.
Scaling the intervention to larger geometries may reduce its effectiveness because of different thermal-management requirements.
